practice.stem:
Read Text A and Text B, then answer the question.

Text A: Phones off, minds on (from a parents' newsletter)

Our school should follow the example of many others and ban mobile phones completely during the school day. Phones would be handed in at the gate each morning and returned at home time.

The reasons are obvious to anyone who has watched a group of teenagers at break. Instead of talking, playing or simply resting their minds, they sit hunched over screens. Teachers tell us that notifications interrupt lessons, and that some pupils secretly message friends or play games under their desks.

Phones also bring the worst of the internet into school. Arguments that begin online continue in the corridors, and cruel photographs can be shared within seconds. A ban would give pupils seven hours a day of freedom from this pressure.

Some parents worry about contacting their children in an emergency. But the school office has always been able to pass on messages, just as it did before phones existed. A short period of adjustment would be worth the calmer, more focused school that would result.

Text B: Don't treat us like children (a student's blog)

Every few months, someone suggests banning phones in school, and every time I want to ask: has anyone asked us?

My phone is not just for games. I use it to check my timetable, photograph the board when I can't copy fast enough, look up words in English lessons and use the calculator in science. During the last power cut, it was the only torch in our classroom.

Banning phones will not stop online bullying. Most of it happens in the evening, at home, where the school has no control. What would actually help is teaching us how to use phones responsibly and how to report problems, because we will have phones for the rest of our lives.

There is also the journey to and from school. Many of us travel by bus or rickshaw, and our parents feel safer knowing they can reach us. Handing phones in at the gate means queues and lost or damaged devices.

A better rule would be simple: phones switched off in lessons unless the teacher asks for them. Trust us, and most of us will respect it.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Your headteacher is considering banning mobile phones during the school day. You decide to write a letter to the headteacher.

In your letter you should:
• evaluate the views given in both texts about banning mobile phones in school
• give your own views, based on what you have read.

Begin your letter, 'Dear Headteacher'.

Base your answer on what you have read in both texts, but be careful to use your own words. Address both of the bullet points. Write about 250 to 350 words. Up to 15 marks are available for the content of your answer and up to 25 marks for the quality of your writing (exam total 40).
parts.answer: Model plan: Opening – purpose (respond to proposal; student perspective). Para 2 – accept Text A's concerns about distraction and the cruelty of shared images, but challenge the claim that a ban gives 'freedom from pressure', since Text B shows bullying mostly happens at home. Para 3 – weigh Text B's educational uses against Text A's evidence of misuse: uses are real but could be supervised. Para 4 – safety on journeys (B) versus office messages (A): office cannot help on the bus. Para 5 – own view: a compromise (phones off and in bags in lessons; used only when teacher permits; clear sanctions; lessons on online safety). Close formally, offering student-council help.
parts.working: Ideas to evaluate: Text A: phones distract at break and in lessons; secret messaging/games; online arguments and cruel photos spread; ban gives relief from pressure; office can pass emergency messages; adjustment worth it. Text B: phones used for timetable, photos of the board, dictionary, calculator, torch; bullying mainly happens out of school; better to teach responsible use; safety on journeys; queues and damage at gate; alternative rule – off in lessons unless asked. Evaluation points: A relies on observation but generalises; B's practical uses could be replaced by school devices; both care about well-being; compromise possible. practice.stem:
Read Text A and Text B, then answer the question.

Text A: Give the bazaar back to people (from a heritage society report)

The old bazaar is one of the city's treasures: a maze of narrow lanes lined with spice merchants, cloth sellers and centuries-old doorways. Yet anyone who tries to walk there today must dodge motorbikes, delivery vans and cars forcing their way through spaces built for donkeys and handcarts.

We propose that the main bazaar street be closed to motor traffic between ten in the morning and eight at night. Deliveries could be made early in the morning. Elsewhere, similar schemes have transformed historic centres: air becomes cleaner, accidents fall, and visitors linger longer and spend more.

Pedestrian streets also protect old buildings, whose fragile walls are shaken by heavy vehicles. They allow space for street food, performers and seating, and they make the bazaar safer for children, elderly people and wheelchair users.

The bazaar has survived for centuries. It will not survive many more decades of traffic jams.

Text B: Who will carry the goods? (a shopkeeper's view)

My family has sold brass and copper in the bazaar for three generations, and I am worried about the plan to ban vehicles.

Many of our customers are not tourists strolling around with cameras. They are wholesalers and families who buy heavy goods: large cooking pots, trays and wedding gifts. They come by car or motorbike and load their purchases at the door. If they have to carry everything half a kilometre to a car park, they will simply shop elsewhere.

Early-morning deliveries sound simple, but our suppliers come from other cities and cannot always arrive before ten. Porters would have to be paid to carry stock, adding to costs that are already high.

There is also a risk that the bazaar becomes a museum for visitors rather than a working market for local people. I agree the traffic is terrible, but the answer is better parking at the edges, strict rules on through traffic and fines for double parking, not a total ban.

parts.text:

practice.stem:
Read Text A and Text B, then answer the question.

Text A: Open-plan offices bring us together (from a property company advertisement)

Gone are the days of grey corridors and closed doors. Our new office buildings are designed around bright, open floors where whole teams work side by side.

Open-plan spaces encourage conversation. When colleagues can see one another, questions are answered in seconds rather than by lengthy emails, and ideas are shared naturally over a desk. Managers are visible and approachable, so problems are spotted early.

These offices are also more flexible. Desks can be rearranged as teams grow or change, and the absence of walls lets natural light reach every corner, which research suggests improves mood. Companies save money, too: the same floor can accommodate more people.

Modern businesses depend on teamwork. Our open-plan offices are built for it.

Text B: I can't hear myself think (an employee's blog)

When my company moved into an open-plan office, we were promised a new era of teamwork. What we got was noise.

Phones ring, people chat, someone eats crisps beside me, and a colleague's video call can be heard across the room. For work that needs real concentration, such as checking figures or writing reports, it is exhausting. Many of us now wear headphones all day, which rather defeats the point of talking to one another.

There is no privacy. Discussing a personal problem with a manager, or making a doctor's appointment, means doing it in a corridor. Illnesses spread more quickly, too; when one person catches a cold, half the floor follows.

I am not asking for my own office. But a few quiet rooms, some screens between desks and agreed silent hours would make a huge difference.

parts.text:
Your employer is planning to move your department into an open-plan office. You decide to write a letter to your manager.

In your letter you should:
• evaluate the views given in both texts about open-plan offices
• give your own views, based on what you have read.

Begin your letter, 'Dear Ms Akhtar'.

Base your answer on what you have read in both texts, but be careful to use your own words. Address both of the bullet points. Write about 250 to 350 words. Up to 15 marks are available for the content of your answer and up to 25 marks for the quality of your writing (exam total 40).

Evaluate B – concrete, believable problems (noise, concentration, privacy, illness); ironically headphones reduce the very conversation open plan promises; constructive suggestions. Own view: accept the move with conditions – quiet rooms, screens, silent hours, private meeting space. Polite professional register.

practice.stem:
Read Text A and Text B, then answer the question.

Text A: A car park we badly need (from a traders' association leaflet)

Shopkeepers on Station Road have struggled for years. Customers circle the block looking for somewhere to park, give up and drive to the new mall on the bypass, where parking is free and plentiful. Half a dozen shops have closed in the last two years alone.

The council now has a simple way to help: turn the small, little-used park behind the post office into a two-level car park. The park is neglected. Its benches are broken, its grass is worn to dust, and after dark it attracts people drinking and littering. Few families use it.

A car park would bring shoppers back, protect jobs and increase the council's income through parking fees, which could then be spent on improving other parks in the town. Some trees would be lost, but new ones could be planted along the edge of the car park.

If we do nothing, Station Road will become a street of shuttered shops. The town centre must come first.

Text B: Save Jinnah Park (a residents' petition)

The council plans to concrete over Jinnah Park, the only green space within walking distance for over two thousand households in the old town. We, the undersigned residents, say no.

Yes, the park is shabby. That is because the council has failed to maintain it for a decade. Mend the benches, water the grass and light the paths, and families will return; we have seen it happen in other districts.

Every morning, elderly residents walk there and children play cricket after school, because there is nowhere else to go. The large trees provide shade on hot afternoons and help clean air that is already heavy with traffic fumes. Once a park is gone, it never comes back.

More parking will simply bring more cars into narrow streets that are already jammed. If shops are struggling, the answer is better buses, a weekly market and pleasant streets that make people want to stroll and shop, not another slab of concrete.

We call on the council to restore the park, not destroy it.

parts.text:
Your local council is deciding whether to turn a small town park into a car park. You decide to write a letter to the council.

In your letter you should:
• evaluate the views given in both texts about replacing the park with a car park
• give your own views, based on what you have read.

Begin your letter, 'Dear Councillors'.

Base your answer on what you have read in both texts, but be careful to use your own words. Address both of the bullet points. Write about 250 to 350 words. Up to 15 marks are available for the content of your answer and up to 25 marks for the quality of your writing (exam total 40).

practice.stem:
Read Text A and Text B, then answer the question.

Text A: The four-day week works (from a business website)

When our design company moved to a four-day working week last year, many clients thought we had gone mad. Twelve months later, the results speak for themselves.

Staff now work Monday to Thursday, for slightly longer hours each day, with no cut in pay. Because everyone knows that Friday is free, meetings are shorter, emails are answered faster and time-wasting has almost disappeared. Our productivity has actually risen.

Sick days have fallen sharply, and staff say they come back on Monday refreshed rather than exhausted. Recruiting has become much easier: when we advertised two jobs in the spring, we received four times as many applications as before.

There are challenges. Some clients expected to reach us on Fridays, so we created a small rota to answer urgent calls. But overall, we are convinced. A rested workforce is a better workforce, and the five-day week is a habit, not a law of nature.

Text B: Four days? Not for everyone (comments from an online forum)

Shazia, nurse: "A four-day week sounds lovely in an office, but hospitals, shops and factories need people every day. If some workers get Fridays off and others don't, resentment builds very quickly."

Daniel, small shop owner: "I employ six people. If each of them works one day less, I either close for a day and lose customers or hire extra staff I can't afford."

Hamza, accountant: "We tried it. The longer days were exhausting, especially for colleagues with young children who had to arrange extra childcare in the evenings. Some people ended up checking emails on Friday anyway, so it wasn't really a day off."

Mehwish, graphic designer: "I love my four-day week. But I know it only works because my job can be measured by results, not hours behind a counter."

practice.stem:
Read Text A and Text B, then answer the question.

Text A: Too many visitors (from an environmental group's website)

Every summer, the narrow road to the lake is jammed with cars for kilometres. Families picnic on the shore, music blares from speakers, and by evening the meadows are littered with plastic bottles, nappies and food wrappers. The lake that once drew visitors with its silence is being loved to death.

We call on the regional authorities to introduce a daily limit on visitors, with tickets booked in advance, and to charge an entrance fee. The money should be used to employ local rangers, build proper toilets and remove rubbish.

Some will say this keeps poorer visitors away, but a modest fee is a small price for protecting the lake. Without limits, the wildlife will disappear, the water will become polluted and visitors will eventually stop coming because the place has been ruined.

Text B: Nature belongs to everyone (a tour guide writes to a local paper)

I have guided visitors to the lake for fifteen years, and I agree that the litter is shameful. But a daily limit and an entrance fee are the wrong answer.

For many families from the cities below, a day at the lake is their only holiday of the year. A fee, especially one charged per person, would make that trip impossible for the very people who most need fresh air and open space. Advance booking also assumes everyone has internet access and can plan weeks ahead.

The local economy depends on visitors. Hotels, tea stalls, jeep drivers and guides like me would lose income if numbers were cut.

The problem is not how many people come but how they behave. Put bins and toilets along the shore, employ wardens to fine people who drop litter, and educate visitors with signs and leaflets. Most people will respect the lake if they are shown how.

parts.text:

Note common ground: both want toilets, rubbish removal and staff. Own view: a combination – free or low-cost entry with limits only at peak weekends, fines for littering, fees for vehicles rather than people, funds for local rangers. Formal letter.

practice.stem:
Read Text A and Text B, then answer the question.

Text A: Let them sleep (from an education magazine)

Research into the teenage body clock has been clear for years: adolescents naturally fall asleep later and need more sleep than adults. Yet many schools still expect pupils to be seated and alert by half past seven.

A later start, perhaps at nine o'clock, would allow teenagers to get closer to the eight or nine hours they need. Schools abroad that have tried this report fewer pupils arriving late, better concentration in morning lessons and improved moods. Some even noticed fewer road accidents among young drivers.

Critics say teenagers would simply stay up even later. But the evidence suggests that most would sleep longer, not shift their whole night. In any case, a fixed early start that leaves pupils exhausted makes no sense if our aim is learning rather than routine.

Changing timetables is difficult, but schools exist for pupils' benefit. It is time we built the school day around the bodies of the young people in it, rather than the habits of the adults who run it.

Text B: A later start? Not so simple (a parent's letter to a newspaper)

I understand the arguments for starting school later, but families like mine would find it almost impossible.

Both my husband and I begin work at eight. At present we drop our children at school on our way. If school began at nine, who would look after them for that hour, and who would collect them when they finished later in the afternoon? Not every family has grandparents nearby.

A later finish also means less time for homework, tuition, sports and helping at home, and in winter children would travel home in the dark. School buses and vans that serve several schools would have to change their routes, and costs would rise.

I also doubt that teenagers would use the extra hour to sleep. My son would simply spend it on his phone at midnight. Surely the answer is better habits: earlier bedtimes, no screens at night and parents who set rules.

Before changing a whole system, schools should consult the families who will have to make it work.

• evaluate the views given in both texts about starting the school day later

Weigh: purpose of school is learning; logistics matter. Own view: trial a smaller shift (e.g. 30–45 minutes), supervised early room for pupils dropped off early, survey families, combine with sleep education. Formal, reasoned tone.

Text A: Everyone should win (from a primary teachers' blog)

Sports day at many schools still follows the old pattern: races, medals and a few children celebrating while the rest trail home feeling like failures. It is time to rethink.

Children who are not naturally sporty often dread the event for weeks. Being publicly beaten in front of parents can put a child off exercise for life, which is the opposite of what we want. A sports day built around team challenges, obstacle courses and personal bests would let every child feel successful.

Cooperation matters more than competition in later life. Most jobs require teamwork, not beating colleagues. Activities in which mixed groups solve problems together teach patience, communication and kindness.

Competitive children can still compete in clubs and inter-school matches. Sports day should be a celebration for all, not a showcase for a few.

Text B: Let them lose (from a sports coach's newspaper column)

I keep reading that school sports days should drop races and winners in case children's feelings are hurt. I could not disagree more.

Losing is part of life. Children will fail exams, miss out on jobs and be beaten in all sorts of contests as adults. A sports day race is a safe place to learn how to lose with dignity and try again. Protecting children from every disappointment does them no favours.

Competition also motivates. Many of the athletes I coach began by trying to beat a classmate on sports day. Take away the chance to win, and you take away a reason to train.

We do not hide spelling test results from pupils who struggle with spelling. Why should sport be different? Children who excel at running deserve their moment, just as children who excel at maths or art deserve theirs.

By all means add team games and fun events. But keep the races.

practice.stem:
Read Text A and Text B, then answer the question.

Text A: Time to scrap the uniform (from a youth magazine)

School uniforms belong to another century. They are expensive, uncomfortable and do nothing to improve learning.

Parents are told that uniforms save money, yet blazers, ties and specially labelled jumpers from a single approved shop often cost far more than ordinary clothes. Children grow quickly, and many families struggle to replace items every year.

Uniforms also stifle individuality. The teenage years are when young people discover who they are, and clothing is one of the main ways they express it. Forcing everyone into identical outfits teaches conformity, not confidence.

Supporters claim uniforms reduce bullying, but children always find differences to tease each other about: shoes, bags, haircuts, phones. A sensible dress code, banning offensive slogans and unsafe items, would achieve everything a uniform does at a fraction of the cost.

Text B: Why I'm glad we wear uniform (a head girl's speech)

When I joined this school, I came from a family that could not afford fashionable clothes. On my first day, in my uniform, I looked exactly like everyone else, and nobody knew. That mattered to me more than I can say.

Without a uniform, every morning becomes a competition. Pupils compare brands and judge each other by what they can afford. A uniform removes that pressure and lets us concentrate on who we are rather than what we wear.

Uniform also gives a sense of belonging. When we travel to competitions, we are proud to represent our school, and people recognise us. It helps us switch into 'school mode' in the morning, just as adults dress for work.

Yes, uniforms can be expensive, but that is a reason to make them cheaper, perhaps through second-hand sales, not to scrap them altogether.

practice.stem:
Read Text A and Text B, then answer the question.

Text A: Homework: an outdated habit? (from a parenting website)

Every evening, millions of children sit at kitchen tables completing worksheets after a full day at school. But is homework actually worth it?

For younger children especially, the evidence that homework improves results is weak. What it does do is cause stress and arguments. Parents who work long hours end up nagging tired children, and pupils without a quiet space or help at home fall further behind those with tutors and educated parents.

Children also need time to play, read for pleasure, help their families and simply rest. These activities develop creativity and independence in ways that another page of sums cannot.

Some countries with excellent school results set very little homework. Perhaps we should follow their lead and let school be for learning and home be for living.

Text B: Why homework still matters (a teacher's view)

I am tired of hearing that homework is pointless. Used well, it is one of the most valuable tools we have.

Learning does not stop when the bell rings. Practising a skill on your own, without a teacher to help, is how you find out whether you have truly understood it. Homework also gives time for tasks that do not fit into a lesson: reading a novel, researching a project, learning vocabulary.

Perhaps most importantly, homework builds habits that students will need at university and work: organising time, meeting deadlines and working independently. Students who never learn these habits at school often struggle badly later.

Bad homework, such as pointless worksheets or hours of copying, should certainly go. But the answer is better homework, not none at all.

Text A: Buy less, choose well (from a sustainability magazine)

Fast fashion has made clothes cheaper than ever. A T-shirt can cost less than a sandwich, and new styles arrive in shops every few weeks. But the true cost is hidden.

Making clothes uses enormous amounts of water and energy, and cheap garments often fall apart after a few washes, ending up in landfill. Many are made by workers paid very little in unsafe factories.

The alternative is simple: buy fewer, better-quality clothes, repair what you have and shop second-hand. Charity shops and online resale sites are full of good clothes at low prices, and buying used saves resources and money.

Fashion should be about expressing yourself, not following a trend that will be forgotten next month.

Text B: Not everyone can afford to be choosy (a reader's reply)

It is easy for well-off writers to tell us to 'buy fewer, better-quality clothes'. For many families, cheap fashion is not a luxury but a necessity.

When you have three growing children, a good-quality jacket that costs five times as much is simply not an option, however long it might last. Second-hand shops are not always nearby, and the best items are snapped up quickly, often by people reselling them for profit.

Cheap clothes also provide jobs. Factory work may be hard, but in many countries it is one of the few ways for women to earn an independent income. Boycotting cheap brands could hurt the very workers we want to help.

By all means, let companies improve conditions and make clothes last longer. But please do not blame ordinary families for doing their best on a tight budget.

Text A: Zoos save species (from a zoo's information leaflet)

Modern zoos are not the prisons of the past. Today's best zoos are centres of conservation, education and research.

Many endangered animals survive today partly because zoos bred them when wild numbers fell dangerously low, and some species have been returned to the wild from zoo populations. Zoos also fund conservation projects in the animals' home countries, protecting habitats and training rangers.

For millions of children, a zoo visit is the only chance to see a tiger or an elephant up close. That experience creates a lifelong love of animals and a desire to protect them, which no documentary can match.

Our keepers and vets study animal health and behaviour, and their knowledge helps wildlife experts around the world. A good zoo is not an alternative to wild nature; it is one of its most important allies.

Text B: Empty the cages (from an animal welfare campaign)

However large the enclosure, a zoo is still a cage. An elephant that would walk many kilometres a day in the wild, or an eagle built to soar, cannot live a natural life behind a fence.

Many zoo animals show signs of distress: pacing, rocking or chewing the bars. Most species kept in zoos are not endangered at all, and very few animals bred in captivity are ever released, because they lack the skills to survive.

If we want to save wildlife, the money spent on keeping animals in cities should go directly to protecting their natural habitats, where whole ecosystems benefit.

As for education, children can learn far more by watching animals behave naturally in high-quality films, or by visiting wildlife sanctuaries that rescue injured animals rather than displaying healthy ones for profit.

Text A: AI is the calculator of our time (from a technology blog)

When calculators appeared in classrooms, people feared that children would never learn arithmetic. Today, AI chatbots are causing the same panic, and the same mistake is being made.

AI tools can explain a difficult idea in several different ways until a student understands it, at any hour of the day. They can suggest how to improve an essay, quiz students before a test and help those who cannot afford private tuition.

Banning these tools will not work; students will use them at home anyway. Schools should teach pupils to use AI wisely: to check its answers, to ask good questions and to use it as a tutor rather than a ghost-writer.

The workplaces our students will enter already use AI every day. Schools that ignore it are preparing pupils for a world that no longer exists.

Text B: Who is doing the thinking? (from a school newsletter)

This term, several teachers noticed something odd: homework essays that were fluent, well organised and strangely similar to one another. Many had been produced by AI.

Writing an essay is not about producing a finished document; it is about the thinking that goes into it. Students who let a machine do that thinking miss the struggle that actually builds understanding. They may receive good marks without learning anything.

AI tools also make mistakes. They can invent facts and references with complete confidence, and students who trust them may learn things that are simply wrong.

There is a question of fairness, too. When some students use AI and others do not, marks no longer reflect real effort or ability.

We are not against technology. But until students can show they understand a topic themselves, AI should stay out of homework.

Text A: Why we should go abroad (from a school trip organiser's leaflet)

Every year our school takes a group of students on a trip abroad, and every year they come back changed.

Seeing famous buildings, tasting new food and hearing other languages brings classroom learning to life. History becomes real when you stand in an ancient city; geography makes sense when you see a glacier with your own eyes.

Travelling with classmates also builds independence and confidence. Students learn to manage money, find their way and cope when plans go wrong, all with teachers nearby for support.

Perhaps most valuable is the experience of meeting people whose lives are very different from our own. In a world that often seems divided, understanding other cultures is not a luxury but a necessity.

Text B: Closer to home (a student's proposal to the school council)

Last year's trip abroad cost more than many families earn in a month. Out of a year group of one hundred and twenty, only twenty students went. The rest were left out, and some felt embarrassed even to talk about it.

I propose that the school spends the same money on a local volunteering week for the whole year group. We could help restore a park, read with children at a primary school, plant trees on the riverbank or assist at an old people's home.

This would teach many of the same things as a trip abroad: teamwork, responsibility, confidence and understanding of people different from ourselves. And the benefits would stay in our own community.

Long-haul flights also produce large amounts of pollution. A local project would be cheaper, fairer and greener. Travel is wonderful, but it should not be the only way a school helps students grow.

Read Text A and Text B, then answer the question.

Text A: Influencers: the new role models (from a marketing magazine)

Ask a group of teenagers who they admire and you are as likely to hear the name of an online creator as a sports star or scientist. This is not necessarily bad news.

Many influencers have built their success from nothing, teaching themselves to film, edit and run a business. They show young people that creativity and hard work can lead to a career without connections or wealth. Some use their platforms to raise money for charity or speak openly about mental health, reaching audiences that traditional campaigns cannot.

Influencers also feel closer than celebrities. Followers can comment, ask questions and receive replies, and many creators share honest accounts of failure as well as success. For a lonely teenager, that sense of connection can be important.

Instead of sneering, adults should help young people choose positive role models online.

Text B: The filtered life (from a psychologist's column)

Teenagers today compare themselves not with classmates but with people whose lives are carefully edited for millions of viewers.

Influencers earn money by selling things, and much of what looks like friendly advice is actually advertising. Young followers may not realise that the skincare routine or the trainers have been paid for. Constant exposure to perfect bodies, luxury holidays and expensive possessions can leave young people feeling ugly, poor and inadequate.

The 'honesty' of creators is often a performance, too. Even a video about a bad day is planned, filmed and edited. And for every influencer who makes a living, thousands try and fail, sometimes abandoning their education in the process.

Role models should be people whose lives young people can see in full: parents, teachers, coaches, older friends.

Read Text A and Text B, then answer the question.

Text A: Take a year out (from a travel company brochure)

After years of exams, many young people head straight to university without stopping to ask whether they are on the right path. A gap year offers the chance to find out.

Volunteering abroad, working, or travelling teaches skills no classroom can: independence, problem-solving, budgeting and dealing with people from different cultures. Students return more mature, more confident and often clearer about what they want to study.

Universities and employers increasingly value these experiences. A student who has taught children in a village school or worked on a conservation project has stories to tell at interview.

Our programmes in more than twenty countries make it easy, with accommodation, support and adventure included. Your future can wait a year. Your adventure cannot.

Text B: Gap years: a privilege, not a plan (from a careers adviser's blog)

Gap years are often presented as life-changing adventures. For some, they are. But we should be more honest about the downsides.

Organised programmes abroad can be extremely expensive, which means they are mainly available to students from wealthy families. Short-term 'volunteering' can even do harm, as when untrained teenagers spend a few weeks in schools or orphanages and then leave.

Some students lose momentum. After a year away from study, returning to academic work can be hard, and a few never go back at all.

A gap year can be valuable if it is planned carefully: working locally to save money, gaining experience related to a future career, or volunteering long-term with a reputable local organisation. Travelling simply because friends are doing it is not a plan.

Text A: Make community service compulsory (from a newspaper editorial)

Every secondary school student should complete forty hours of community service before leaving school.

Young people have energy and skills that our communities badly need. Hospitals, libraries, animal shelters and clean-up campaigns are always short of helpers. At the same time, many teenagers spend hours each day on screens, cut off from the people around them.

Volunteering teaches responsibility, empathy and teamwork, and it introduces young people to careers they may never have considered. It also breaks down barriers between generations: an afternoon spent with elderly residents can change a teenager's view of old age.

Making it compulsory ensures that every student benefits, not just those whose parents already encourage volunteering.

Text B: Forced kindness isn't kindness (a student's letter)

I volunteer every Saturday at an animal shelter, and I love it. But I strongly oppose making community service compulsory.

Volunteering means choosing to give your time. When it becomes a requirement, students will do the minimum, watch the clock and treat it as another box to tick. Organisations would have to supervise unwilling teenagers, which takes staff away from real work.

Many students already help their communities in ways that are not counted: caring for younger siblings, working in family shops or looking after sick grandparents. Adding forty hours to their workload, especially in exam years, is unfair.

Encourage volunteering, celebrate it, make it easy to find opportunities. But do not force it.

Text A: No smartphone before fourteen (a parents' campaign leaflet)

More and more parents are agreeing to wait until their children are at least fourteen before giving them a smartphone.

Young children are not ready for the internet in their pocket. Smartphones expose them to harmful content, contact with strangers and endless games and videos designed to keep them hooked. Sleep, homework and outdoor play suffer.

Children can still have a simple phone for calls and texts, so parents can stay in touch. If enough families agree to wait together, no child need feel left out.

Childhood is short. Let children enjoy it before they enter the online world.

Text B: Banning isn't parenting (a parent's blog)

I understand the worries about smartphones, but I disagree with banning them until fourteen.

My daughter got her first smartphone at eleven. We agreed rules together: no phone at meals or after nine, parental controls, and she tells me if anything online upsets her. She uses it to video-call her grandparents abroad, practise languages and coordinate with friends.

Children who never use smartphones until fourteen suddenly receive one without any experience or guidance, which may be more dangerous. And in many classes, important information is shared in group chats; a child without a phone can genuinely miss out.

Rather than banning, we should be teaching children to use technology safely while we are still there to guide them.

Text A: A mall means jobs (from a developer's presentation)

Our proposed shopping mall on the edge of town will bring more than one hundred shops, a cinema, restaurants and a children's play area under one roof.

Construction alone will employ hundreds of local workers, and once open, the mall will provide around eight hundred permanent jobs, many of them suitable for young people. Local businesses will be offered units at reduced rents in the first year.

Families currently drive to the city, an hour away, for this kind of shopping and entertainment. The mall will keep that money in our town. It will also be air-conditioned, safe and clean, with plenty of parking.

The site is ordinary farmland. A modern town needs modern facilities.

Text B: Don't pave our fields (from a farmers' and residents' group)

The land chosen for the mall is not 'ordinary farmland'. It produces wheat and vegetables for local markets, and families have farmed it for generations. Once concrete is poured, it can never be farmed again.

The jobs promised are mostly low-paid shop work, while small traders in the town centre, already struggling, may lose customers to the mall and close. We could end up with a busy mall and an empty town centre.

Traffic is another concern. Hundreds of cars on narrow rural roads will bring noise, pollution and danger to villages along the route. Heavy rain already floods these fields; building over them could push water into nearby homes.

We support development, but it should use empty buildings and land already built on, not destroy the farms that feed us.

Text A: Ban plastic bags in the market (from a city environment officer's report)

Our weekly market uses tens of thousands of thin plastic bags every day. Most are used for a few minutes and then thrown away. They block drains, causing flooding in the monsoon, and they are eaten by cattle and goats that wander the streets.

We recommend banning thin plastic bags in the market from next year. Cloth and jute bags are cheap, strong and can be reused hundreds of times. Other cities that introduced similar bans have seen cleaner streets and fewer blocked drains within months.

Shoppers adapt quickly once bringing a bag becomes a habit. Small changes by many people can make a big difference.

Text B: Think of the small sellers (a vegetable seller's view)

I sell vegetables in the market six days a week. My customers expect a bag, and if I don't give one, they buy from the next stall.

Paper bags tear when tomatoes are wet, and cloth bags cost me far more than plastic. If I have to provide them, my small profit disappears. If I ask customers to pay, they complain.

When bans have been tried before, plastic bags were still sold secretly, and the shopkeepers who obeyed the rules lost out. The real problem is the lack of bins and rubbish collection. Clean the drains, provide bins, and the bags will not end up in the streets.

I am not against protecting the environment. But please do not make the poorest traders pay for it.

Text A: Car-free streets around schools (a road safety charity's proposal)

Every morning, the streets outside our schools turn into car parks. Parents double-park, reverse onto pavements and leave engines running, while children squeeze between bumpers.

We propose 'school streets': roads outside schools closed to cars for half an hour at the start and end of the school day. Residents and disabled drivers would still have access.

Where this has been tried, more children walk, cycle or scoot to school, air pollution at the gates falls, and accidents decrease. Children arrive more alert after exercise, and parents chat on the walk instead of fighting for parking spaces.

The safety of children must come before the convenience of drivers.

School streets sound wonderful if you live around the corner. But many families do not.

I drop my two children at different schools on my way to work, which starts at eight. Without the car, I cannot do it. Public transport in our area is unreliable, and walking two kilometres along a busy main road is hardly safer for young children.

Closing the street will simply push the same cars into neighbouring roads, causing jams and anger among residents there. Children with disabilities, or those who live far away, would be hit hardest.

Instead, provide a supervised drop-off zone a short walk away, safer crossings and a school bus. Help families who cannot walk, rather than punishing them.

Text A: Talent shows open doors (from an entertainment website)

Television talent shows have launched the careers of singers, dancers and comedians who might otherwise never have been discovered. For a young performer from a small town, a single appearance can mean being seen by millions.

The shows also give ordinary viewers a voice: audiences vote, and sometimes the winner is someone the judges overlooked. Contestants receive coaching from professionals, perform on a huge stage and learn to cope with pressure.

Even those who do not win often gain followers, bookings and confidence. And for families watching at home, talent shows are a rare programme that everyone, from grandparents to toddlers, enjoys together.

Text B: The cost of the spotlight (from a former contestant's memoir)

I was sixteen when I reached the semi-final of a talent show, and for three weeks I was famous. Then I was voted out, and within a month nobody remembered my name.

What viewers do not see is how much is edited. My nervousness was turned into a 'tearful breakdown' for the cameras, and producers encouraged arguments between contestants because conflict made good television. Online comments about my weight and my accent were brutal.

Winners often sign contracts that give the programme a large share of their earnings. Many are dropped after a single record.

Young performers are better served by local theatres, music schools and steady practice, where they can grow without being judged by millions before they are ready.

Text A: Reach for the stars (from a science magazine)

Space exploration is sometimes described as a waste of money while problems remain on Earth. This view misunderstands what space programmes give back.

Satellites provide weather forecasts that warn of cyclones and floods, help farmers plan their harvests and allow phones and navigation systems to work. Technologies developed for space travel have led to improvements in medicine, water purification and materials we use every day.

Space missions also inspire. Many scientists and engineers say they chose their careers after watching a launch as a child. Studying other planets helps us understand our own climate and the risks it faces.

Spending on space is a tiny fraction of most countries' budgets. It is an investment in knowledge, not a luxury.

Text B: Fix the Earth first (from a charity's newsletter)

Every time a rocket launches, millions of people around the world still lack clean water, enough food or a nearby hospital. Billions are spent on missions to Mars while children die of preventable diseases.

Some argue that space research brings practical benefits. But if we want better medicine or clean water, it would be cheaper to fund that research directly rather than hoping it emerges from rocket programmes.

Increasingly, space is becoming a playground for the very rich, with private companies selling short trips to wealthy tourists. Rocket launches also burn huge amounts of fuel.

Exploring space can wait. Our most urgent mission is here on Earth.

Imagine a month without social media. Many people who have tried a 'digital detox' say it changed their lives.

Without constant notifications, they slept better, concentrated for longer and felt less anxious. They read books, rediscovered hobbies and spent real time with friends instead of scrolling through other people's highlights.

Text B: Balance, not escape (a psychologist's advice)

Complete digital detoxes are fashionable, but they rarely last. Most people return to their old habits within weeks, sometimes using their phones even more to catch up on what they missed.

For many young people, social media is also how they keep in touch with friends, find out about events and get support. Cutting off completely can leave them feeling isolated, especially if friends continue to communicate online.

A better approach is to change how we use technology: turning off notifications, setting time limits, keeping phones out of bedrooms and unfollowing accounts that make us feel bad. Small, lasting changes beat dramatic gestures.

Text: The kite on the roof

(1) My grandfather's house in the old city had a flat roof, and every spring, on the morning of the kite festival, the whole family climbed the narrow stairs before breakfast. I was nine that year and had been promised, at last, that I could fly a kite of my own.

(2) From the roof the city looked like a crowded chessboard of other roofs, each one alive with people. Music thudded from loudspeakers somewhere to the east. Above us the sky was already freckled with kites: paper diamonds in lime green and hot pink, swooping and stalling like nervous birds, their strings glinting in the low sun. The air smelled of fried pakoras, diesel and the dusty sweetness of marigolds strung along the parapet.

(3) Grandfather handed me the reel as if it were something precious. "Let the wind do the work," he said. "You only listen." I ran three steps, the kite lifted, dipped, and then — miraculously — climbed, tugging at my fingers like a small animal desperate to escape.

(4) For a few minutes I was a king. My kite, purple with a white tail, rode higher and higher until it was a tiny flickering stamp against the blue. Then another kite slid towards it, sly as a crocodile in a river, and the two strings crossed. My line went taut, hummed, and suddenly fell limp in my hands. I watched my kite drift away over the rooftops, turning slowly, already somebody else's prize, while shouts of triumph rose from a roof three streets away. Something hot and heavy climbed into my throat.

(5) I expected to be laughed at. Instead, Grandfather sat down beside me on an upturned bucket and began to tell me about the first kite he had lost, sixty years earlier, on the same roof. By the time he finished, my tears had dried, and he had quietly tied a new kite to my reel.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Reread paragraphs 2 and 4.
• Paragraph 2: the view from the roof on the morning of the festival.
• Paragraph 4: the narrator's kite being cut free.

Explain how the writer uses language to convey meaning and to create effect in these paragraphs. Choose three examples of words or phrases from each paragraph to support your answer. Your choices should include the use of imagery. Write about 200 to 300 words.
parts.answer:
Paragraph 2: The city is 'a crowded chessboard of other roofs', an image that suggests a vast pattern of squares seen from above and hints at a game about to be played, fitting the competitive kite-flying. The sky is 'freckled with kites', a gentle image that makes the kites seem like countless small spots of colour scattered across a face, suggesting how many there are and the cheerful, natural feel of the festival. They swoop 'like nervous birds', which makes them seem alive and unpredictable, hinting at the danger ahead. The mix of smells ('fried pakoras, diesel and the dusty sweetness of marigolds') appeals to the senses and conveys a crowded, joyful, slightly chaotic scene.
Paragraph 4: 'I was a king' shows the child's sense of power and pride. The kite becomes 'a tiny flickering stamp', showing how high it has climbed and how fragile it now looks. The rival kite slides 'sly as a crocodile in a river', a menacing simile suggesting a hidden predator that strikes silently, so the reader senses the attack before the narrator does. The line 'hummed' then 'fell limp', a sudden change from tension to emptiness that mirrors the child's disappointment. 'Something hot and heavy climbed into my throat' conveys tears and humiliation physically, without naming the feeling.
Overall, the writer moves from colour and excitement to loss, making the grandfather's kindness in paragraph 5 more touching.

Text: Shinjuku at eight

(1) My cousin had warned me that the station would be busy, but no warning could have prepared me. I had been in Tokyo for exactly one day, my Japanese consisted of four polite phrases, and I had to change trains at eight o'clock on a Monday morning.

(2) The moment the doors opened, the crowd carried me out like a leaf on a fast river. Thousands of people in dark suits moved in every direction at once, yet nobody collided; they flowed around one another with the silent precision of a shoal of fish. Announcements chimed overhead in a bright, cheerful voice I could not understand, and signs in three alphabets flashed and scrolled until my eyes ached.

(3) I stopped to look at my phone and was immediately an obstacle. A man swerved, murmured something apologetic, and was gone. I stepped against a pillar and tried to find the platform number my cousin had written on a scrap of paper.

(4) The map on the wall was a tangle of coloured lines, like a plate of noodles dropped on the floor. I traced one with my finger, lost it, and traced it again. My heart was hammering, and my shirt stuck to my back. All around me the river of people kept rushing past, indifferent and endless, and I felt suddenly very small, a single grain of rice in an enormous bowl. I thought about my mother telling me I was not ready to travel alone, and about how much I had wanted to prove her wrong.

(5) Then an elderly woman with a shopping trolley stopped beside me. She looked at my piece of paper, nodded, and without a word set off, glancing back to make sure I was following. She led me up two escalators and along a corridor to the right platform, bowed, and disappeared into the crowd before I could even thank her properly.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Reread paragraphs 2 and 4.
• Paragraph 2: the narrator's first moments in the crowd.
• Paragraph 4: the narrator trying to read the map.

Explain how the writer uses language to convey meaning and to create effect in these paragraphs. Choose three examples of words or phrases from each paragraph to support your answer. Your choices should include the use of imagery. Write about 200 to 300 words.
parts.answer:
Paragraph 2: 'The crowd carried me out like a leaf on a fast river' shows the narrator's helplessness: the narrator is light, small and swept along by an uncontrollable force. 'Thousands of people … moved in every direction at once' conveys the overwhelming scale. Yet they flow 'with the silent precision of a shoal of fish', an image suggesting perfect, instinctive coordination, which contrasts with the narrator, the only one who does not know the pattern. The announcements in a 'bright, cheerful voice I could not understand' are ironic: cheerful for others, meaningless to the narrator. Signs that 'flashed and scrolled until my eyes ached' show sensory overload.
Paragraph 4: The map 'like a plate of noodles dropped on the floor' is a humorous but vivid simile for a confusing tangle of lines. 'Traced one … lost it, and traced it again' uses repetition to show the narrator's frustration. 'Heart was hammering' and 'shirt stuck to my back' give physical signs of panic. The crowd is a 'river of people … indifferent and endless', continuing the earlier image and stressing that nobody notices the narrator. 'A single grain of rice in an enormous bowl' conveys how insignificant and lost the narrator feels. The memory of the mother's warning adds pride and self-doubt.
Overall, the writer builds a sense of isolation so that the old woman's quiet kindness has more impact.

Text: Fog at the junction

(1) The train from Lahore was due at the small junction at nine in the evening. At eleven, the stationmaster wrote "Late" on the blackboard in chalk and went back into his office. By midnight, nobody even looked at the board any more.

(2) The fog had come down at dusk, thick and silent, swallowing first the fields, then the signal post, then the far end of the platform. The single lamp above the ticket window wore a fuzzy halo of light, and beyond it the world simply stopped, as if someone had hung a dirty grey curtain across the tracks. Every so often a figure would loom out of the whiteness, a porter with a trolley or a man wrapped in a blanket, and dissolve again a few steps later like a ghost walking through a wall.

(3) About twenty passengers waited on the benches. A family shared roti from a cloth bundle; a student slept with his head on his rucksack; two old men played cards by the light of a mobile phone. The tea seller, who should have gone home hours before, kept his little stove alight and refilled cups without being asked.

(4) The cold was the worst of it. It seeped up from the concrete through the soles of my shoes and crept inside my sleeves and collar, patient and determined. My fingers ached around the hot glass of tea. Somewhere out in the fog a dog barked, once, and the sound seemed to come from everywhere at once. When a train whistle finally sounded, faint and far away, the whole platform held its breath; heads lifted like birds hearing a hawk.

(5) It was a goods train, rattling slowly through without stopping. Nobody complained. The tea seller simply put more water on to boil, and one of the card players began, very softly, to sing.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Reread paragraphs 2 and 4.
• Paragraph 2: the fog at the station.
• Paragraph 4: the cold and the sound of a whistle.

Explain how the writer uses language to convey meaning and to create effect in these paragraphs. Choose three examples of words or phrases from each paragraph to support your answer. Your choices should include the use of imagery. Write about 200 to 300 words.
parts.answer:
Paragraph 2: The fog is 'thick and silent', and it is personified as 'swallowing first the fields, then the signal post, then the far end of the platform', a list that shows its steady advance and makes it seem like a creature eating the world. The lamp 'wore a fuzzy halo of light', suggesting softness and isolation. 'As if someone had hung a dirty grey curtain across the tracks' conveys how completely the world ends beyond the platform, with 'dirty' giving an unpleasant tone. Figures 'loom' and 'dissolve … like a ghost walking through a wall', creating an eerie, dreamlike atmosphere.
Paragraph 4: 'The cold was the worst of it' is blunt and direct. Cold 'seeped up' and 'crept', personified as 'patient and determined', making it seem like an enemy that cannot be resisted. Fingers that 'ached around the hot glass' show the contrast of warmth and cold. The dog's bark that 'seemed to come from everywhere at once' shows how the fog distorts sound and adds unease. When the whistle sounds, 'the whole platform held its breath', personifying the crowd as one body united by hope, and 'heads lifted like birds hearing a hawk' captures their sudden alertness.
Overall, the writer creates a mood of weary, shared waiting, which makes the anticlimax of the goods train, and the kindness of the tea seller, more effective.

Text: Halfway across the lake

(1) The lake swim was two kilometres, from the boathouse to the jetty on the far shore. Sana had trained for it in the school pool all winter, length after length beneath the buzzing lights, but she had never swum in open water further than she could stand.

(2) At the start, the water was a shock: cold enough to snatch the breath from her lungs, and dark, so that her own hands vanished a few centimetres below the surface. Around her, two hundred swimmers churned forward in a frenzy of arms and white foam, like a pot coming to the boil. Someone's heel struck her shoulder; someone else swam straight over her legs. She swallowed a mouthful of the lake, which tasted of mud and weeds, and came up coughing.

(3) Gradually the crowd thinned out. She found a rhythm — breathe, stroke, stroke, breathe — and began to sight on the yellow buoys that marked the course, lifting her eyes every few strokes the way her coach had shown her.

(4) Halfway across, her left calf seized. The pain was sudden and savage, as though a fist had clenched around the muscle and was twisting it. Her leg became a useless weight dragging her down. Panic rose in her like floodwater, and for a second she thrashed, gulping air and water together. The far shore looked impossibly distant, a thin green line wobbling on the horizon. Then she rolled onto her back, as she had been taught, and floated, staring up at a sky so wide and calm that it seemed to be holding her up. A kayak glided alongside, and a steward asked if she wanted to be pulled out.

(5) She shook her head. When the cramp eased, she turned over and swam on, slowly, favouring the leg. She finished in the last twenty, shivering and grinning, and her father, waiting on the jetty, wrapped her in a towel without saying a word.

Text: Service

(1) On her first evening as a trainee in the kitchen of a large hotel in Dubai, Mariam was given a knife, a mountain of onions and a single instruction: "Don't get in anyone's way." By seven o'clock, she understood why.

(2) When the first orders arrived, the kitchen exploded into life. Flames leapt from the pans with a roar, licking upwards towards the extractor fans. Chefs shouted orders across the steel counters in four languages, and the printer by the pass chattered out ticket after ticket like a machine gun that would never run out of bullets. Waiters swept in and out through the swinging doors, and every surface hissed, clattered or steamed. The heat was astonishing; within minutes Mariam's white jacket was soaked through.

(3) The head chef, a tall Sri Lankan man named Ruwan, moved through the chaos without ever seeming to hurry. He tasted everything, said very little, and occasionally pushed a plate back towards a cook with one finger, which was worse than any shout.

(4) At eight, a chef on the sauce station burned his hand and was sent to the first-aid room, and Ruwan pointed at Mariam. "You. Stir. Don't stop." She found herself in front of a huge pan of sauce that bubbled and spat like a small volcano, its surface glossy and dark as melted chocolate. Her arm ached after five minutes and burned after ten. Around her, the noise rose and fell like waves crashing on rocks, but she kept her eyes on the pan and her spoon moving in slow figures of eight, terrified that if she stopped for a second, the whole thing would catch and burn.

(5) At eleven, the last ticket was cleared. Ruwan walked past, dipped a spoon into her pan, tasted it, and nodded once. Mariam had never been so tired, or so happy.

Text: The water came at four

(1) It had been raining since lunchtime, but nobody in our street worried. Rain in July is normal, and the drains usually managed. I was walking home from tuition with my bag over my head when I noticed that the gutters were no longer gutters but small brown rivers.

(2) By the time I reached the main road, the water was over my ankles and rising. Cars ploughed through it like reluctant buffaloes, pushing waves onto the pavement, and a rickshaw had stalled in the middle of the junction, its driver standing on the seat and shouting at nobody. Plastic bags, sandals and a child's ball spun past me. The sky had turned the colour of a bruise, and the rain no longer fell in drops but in heavy grey ropes that stung my face.

(3) I tried to remember the safest way home. The lane behind the bakery was lower, so I kept to the main road, holding on to railings and shop shutters, testing each step before trusting it. Somewhere an uncovered manhole was waiting; everyone knew the stories.

(4) At the corner of our street the water reached my knees, warm and thick and stinking of diesel. Our neighbour, old Mrs Zaidi, stood in her doorway clutching a birdcage to her chest, her face as white as flour. Her front room had become a pond; a cushion floated across it as slowly as a lazy duck. I waded over and took her arm. Her fingers gripped mine like the claws of a frightened bird, and together we edged along the wall towards our house, which stood two steps higher.

(5) That night, eleven of us slept on our first floor, with Mrs Zaidi's canary singing in the corner as though nothing had happened. In the morning the water had gone, leaving behind a crust of mud and a smell that lasted for weeks.

Text: White-out

(1) We were two hours from the base camp, and the glacier had been kind to us all morning: firm snow, clear sky, the peaks around us so sharp against the blue that they looked as if they had been cut out with scissors. Ayesha, our guide, kept glancing at the west, but she said nothing.

(2) The cloud arrived quickly. First a thin veil slid over the ridge; then the sun became a pale coin, then a smudge, and then it was gone. Within minutes the world had been rubbed out. Snow and sky merged into one blank, milky wall, and I could not tell up from down. The only colours left were the red of Ayesha's jacket, three metres ahead, and the blue rope between us, which suddenly seemed as thin as a thread of cotton.

(3) "Stop," she called. "Nobody moves." We gathered close, roped together, while she checked the compass and the map she had studied the night before. Somewhere to our left, I knew, the glacier was split by crevasses deep enough to swallow a house.

(4) The wind rose and the snow came at us sideways, hissing like sand against our goggles. My fingers, even inside two pairs of gloves, felt like lumps of wood. Every sound was swallowed by the whiteness; when I shouted to the man behind me, my voice seemed to fall at my feet. I began to imagine shapes in the blankness, a tent, a rock, a figure waving, and each one dissolved as soon as I looked at it. Fear crept up my spine with cold little fingers.

(5) Ayesha led us forward one careful step at a time, probing the snow with her pole. It took four hours to cover a distance we had walked in one that morning. When the tents of the camp finally appeared, like small orange lanterns in the mist, nobody cheered. We were too tired, and too grateful, to speak.

'Fear crept up my spine with cold little fingers' personifies fear as a creature, linking emotional and physical cold.

Text: The audition

(1) The corridor outside the audition room was painted a sickly shade of green, and the chairs along the wall were so hard that every candidate sat on the very edge of them. Zara had been waiting for forty minutes. Her violin case lay across her knees, and she kept opening and closing the clasp without noticing she was doing it.

(2) Through the closed door came the sound of the boy before her, playing the same piece she would play. His notes were clean and confident, each one landing exactly where it should, like stones dropped into a still pool. Zara's stomach tightened into a fist. She had practised for six months, two hours every evening, until her neighbours knew the piece as well as she did. Now it seemed to be evaporating from her memory note by note.

(3) The door opened. "Zara Hussain?" A woman with a clipboard smiled briefly and held the door. Inside, three judges sat behind a long table, a glass of water in front of each of them, their faces polite and unreadable.

(4) She lifted the violin to her chin. Her hands were trembling so much that the bow skittered on the first note, a thin squeak like a door hinge, and she saw one judge write something down. For a terrible moment the room tilted. Then she remembered her teacher's advice: play to one person, not to the room. She thought of her grandmother, who had sold a gold bangle to buy this violin, and closed her eyes. The next note was warm and full. The melody rose, steadied, and began to sing, filling the bare room like light pouring through a window.

(5) When she finished, there was a short silence. The judge in the middle took off his glasses. "Thank you," he said. "You may go." It was only in the corridor, as the next candidate stood up, that Zara noticed he had been smiling.

Then the music is 'warm and full', and the melody 'rose, steadied, and began to sing', a sequence of verbs showing growing confidence; personifying the melody as singing suggests it has come alive. 'Filling the bare room like light pouring through a window' makes the sound seem to transform the room, replacing fear with brightness.

Text: The house on Mall Road

(1) I had not been back to the house for twenty years. After my grandmother died, it was locked and left while my uncles argued about who should have it, and somehow the argument outlived two of them. When I finally pushed open the gate, it groaned on its hinges as if it resented being woken.

(2) The garden that I remembered as a jungle of roses and guavas had surrendered completely. Weeds stood waist-high, brittle and grey in the winter sun, and a creeper had wrapped itself around the verandah pillars like a python squeezing its prey. The fountain where my cousins and I had sailed paper boats was cracked and dry, its basin filled with dead leaves the colour of old tea.

(3) The key turned stiffly. Inside, the air was cool and stale and smelled of dust and something sweeter, perhaps the ghost of my grandmother's rosewater. Sheets covered the furniture, so that the drawing room looked like a gathering of patient, shrouded figures waiting for someone to speak.

(4) I went upstairs to the room where I used to sleep during the summer holidays. The window still had the crack shaped like a lightning bolt, and the afternoon light came through it in a thin golden blade that cut across the floor. Dust motes drifted in it, slow and dreamy, like tiny swimmers. On the wall, faint pencil marks recorded my height at seven, eight and nine years old, each line labelled in my grandmother's careful, looping hand. I put my palm flat against them. The plaster was cold, and for a moment my throat closed so tightly that I could not breathe.

(5) Outside, a car horn sounded, and the spell broke. I took a photograph of the pencil marks, locked the door again and walked back down the path through the whispering weeds, knowing that I would not come back.

Text: The dry river

(1) For as long as Imran could remember, the river below his village had been the centre of every summer. Boys swam there, women washed clothes on the flat stones, and in the afternoons he drove the family's three buffaloes down to wallow in the shallows until only their noses and curved horns showed above the water.

(2) That June, the river did not come. Week after week the heat pressed down on the plain like a heavy hand. The sky was white rather than blue, and the sun hung in it like a hot coin. Where the water should have been, there was only a wide bed of cracked mud, split into a crazy pattern of plates that curled at the edges like old paper. The reeds along the bank had turned brittle and brown, and they rattled in the hot wind like dry bones.

(3) The buffaloes suffered most. They stood in the shade of the neem tree with their heads low, panting, and refused to eat. Imran's father poured buckets of water from the well over their backs each morning, but the well too was getting lower, and the water came up cloudy.

(4) One afternoon Imran walked the buffaloes three kilometres downstream, where an old man had told him a pool still remained beneath the railway bridge. The track was white with dust that rose in choking clouds around the animals' hooves. Sweat stung his eyes. When at last he saw the pool, it was a shrunken brown puddle, its edges trampled into thick mud by goats and cattle from five villages. The buffaloes lumbered into it with groans of pleasure, and Imran sat on the bank, watching the water shrink a little more with every hour.

(5) That evening the radio reported that the rains were expected in ten days. His father switched it off without comment and went out to check the well again.

The sky 'white rather than blue' and the sun 'like a hot coin' create a harsh, bleached picture. The mud is 'split into a crazy pattern of plates that curled at the edges like old paper', a precise image of dryness and age, with 'crazy' suggesting disorder. The reeds that 'rattled in the hot wind like dry bones' is a deathly simile suggesting that the land itself is dying.
Paragraph 4: The track is 'white with dust that rose in choking clouds', emphasising the suffocating conditions. 'Sweat stung his eyes' makes the reader feel his discomfort. The pool is a 'shrunken brown puddle', the adjectives destroying the hope built up by the old man's words. Its edges 'trampled into thick mud by … five villages' conveys how many depend on so little water. The buffaloes 'lumbered … with groans of pleasure', a moment of relief, but Imran watches 'the water shrink a little more with every hour', ending on a note of slow, inevitable loss.
Overall, the writer uses images of death and decay to show the seriousness of the drought for the family.

Text: The night the ground moved

(1) My cousin Hina's wedding was held in a marquee in the garden of her parents' house in Quetta. By ten at night, four hundred guests were seated at round tables beneath strings of fairy lights, and the air was warm with the smell of roasting meat and the sound of a band that played slightly too loud.

(2) The marquee was a palace of colour. Its walls were draped in silk of deep red and gold, and chandeliers of fake crystal hung from the roof, scattering little rainbows across the faces below. Hina sat on a raised stage, glittering like a jewel box in her heavy embroidered dress, so still and serious that she might have been a painting. Children chased each other between the tables, and the aunties' laughter rose in bursts like flocks of startled pigeons.

(3) I was carrying a plate of sweets to my grandmother when the first tremor came. It was not dramatic: a low rumble, almost below hearing, and a faint shiver in the floor, as if a heavy lorry were passing in the street.

(4) Then the chandeliers began to sway. Slowly at first, then wildly, like pendulums gone mad, and the fairy lights flickered and danced. Glasses chattered against one another on the tables. A great groan seemed to rise out of the earth itself, deep and animal, and the ground beneath my feet rolled like the deck of a ship. For a second nobody moved. Then four hundred chairs scraped back at once, and the music stopped in the middle of a note. My grandmother caught hold of my wrist with a grip like iron and steered me calmly towards the open side of the marquee.

(5) It lasted less than a minute. Out on the lawn, under the cold stars, we counted heads and found everyone safe. After an hour, when no more tremors came, the band picked up their instruments again, and Hina, still in her glittering dress, laughed for the first time all evening.

Paragraph 2: The marquee is 'a palace of colour', a metaphor suggesting grandeur and celebration. Chandeliers 'scattering little rainbows' create a magical, joyful mood. Hina is 'glittering like a jewel box', a simile suggesting she is precious and richly decorated, but also perhaps stiff and enclosed; 'so still and serious that she might have been a painting' hints at her nerves. The aunties' laughter rising 'like flocks of startled pigeons' is lively and comic, though 'startled' quietly foreshadows the alarm to come.
Paragraph 4: The chandeliers sway 'like pendulums gone mad', turning a symbol of celebration into one of danger and loss of control. Lights that 'flickered and danced' and glasses that 'chattered' are personified, as if the objects themselves are frightened. 'A great groan seemed to rise out of the earth itself, deep and animal' makes the earthquake a living creature, terrifying and primitive. The ground 'rolled like the deck of a ship' conveys instability. 'For a second nobody moved' creates a moment of frozen shock before 'four hundred chairs scraped back at once', showing sudden collective panic. The music stopping 'in the middle of a note' marks the abrupt end of celebration, while the grandmother's 'grip like iron' and calm steering show strength.
Overall, the writer contrasts celebration and terror so that the relief and Hina's laughter at the end feel warm.

Text: First night at sea

(1) Bilal was fifteen when his uncle finally agreed to take him out on the boat. They left Gwadar harbour as the sun was setting, the engine coughing and then settling into a steady growl, and Bilal stood at the bow feeling the spray on his face and trying to look as though he did this every day.

(2) The sea was calm at first, a vast sheet of beaten copper that turned purple, then black, as the light drained away. The coast shrank behind them to a string of yellow beads. Bilal had never known darkness like it: the stars were not scattered but poured across the sky like spilled sugar, and the wake behind the boat glittered with tiny sparks of green light.

(3) Around midnight they put out the nets. His uncle and the two crewmen worked without talking, their hands moving as if they belonged to one body, while Bilal fumbled with ropes that were wet, heavy and seemed determined to tangle. His palms burned. Nobody shouted at him, which somehow made it worse.

(4) Then the wind changed. It came from nowhere, slapping the boat sideways, and the sea, so obedient an hour before, began to heave and snarl. Waves rose like dark hills and broke over the side, drenching him. The deck tilted beneath his feet and his stomach lurched with it. He clung to the mast, sick and terrified, certain the boat would roll over and swallow them all. Through the roar he heard his uncle laughing. "This is nothing!" he shouted. "This is the sea saying hello."

(5) By dawn the wind had dropped, and the nets came up silver and thrashing with fish. Bilal hauled with the others until his arms shook. When the harbour appeared again, low and pale on the horizon, he realised he was no longer pretending.

The coast becomes 'a string of yellow beads', showing how small and distant safety has become. The stars 'poured across the sky like spilled sugar' is a homely simile that conveys their sheer number and the boy's wonder, and the wake 'glittered with tiny sparks of green light' creates a magical, almost enchanted mood. Bilal is awed and peaceful.
Paragraph 4: 'From nowhere' conveys suddenness. The wind 'slapping' the boat personifies it as a bully. The sea, 'so obedient an hour before', now 'began to heave and snarl': it is personified as a tame animal turning savage, so the reader feels the threat as alive and hostile. 'Waves rose like dark hills' conveys their enormous size and weight. His stomach 'lurched' with the deck, linking his fear to the movement physically. 'Certain the boat would roll over and swallow them' shows his terror; ironically, the uncle's 'laughing' and 'This is the sea saying hello' reveal how inexperienced Bilal still is.
Overall, the contrast between beauty and violence shows the sea's double nature and prepares for Bilal's growth.

Text: Frost in the orchard

(1) Every April, Bibi Gul's apricot trees burst into flower all at once, and for a week the terraced orchard above the village looked as though a cloud had come down to rest on the hillside. She was seventy-eight and had planted half the trees herself, carrying the saplings up from the river in a basket on her back.

(2) That year the blossom was the best anyone could remember. The branches were heavy with it, pale pink and white, and when the wind blew, petals drifted down onto the stone walls like warm snow. Bees hummed in the trees from dawn until dusk, a low contented sound like a kettle about to boil, and the whole slope smelled faintly of honey and almonds.

(3) Then the radio warned of a frost. Bibi Gul listened in silence, her hands folded in her lap, and then she sent her grandsons to collect every old tyre, dry branch and sack of sawdust they could find.

(4) By nightfall the sky was hard and clear, and the cold came down from the glacier like a thief. Stars glittered above the peaks, sharp as broken glass. The family lit small smoky fires between the rows of trees and kept them burning hour after hour, feeding them, coughing in the bitter smoke. Bibi Gul moved from fire to fire wrapped in her shawl, a small bent shape in the orange glow, touching the trunks of the trees as if she were comforting children. Her breath hung in front of her face like a ghost. Nobody slept.

(5) At sunrise the grass was white and stiff, crunching underfoot. Some of the lower trees had lost their flowers, the petals brown and curled. But on the higher terraces, where the smoke had lain thickest, the blossom had survived. Bibi Gul stood among the branches for a long time, saying nothing at all.

Petals drifting 'like warm snow' is a paradox: snow is cold, but 'warm' makes the image gentle and beautiful while quietly foreshadowing the real frost to come. The bees' hum, 'a low contented sound like a kettle about to boil', is homely and peaceful, suggesting comfort and contentment, though 'about to boil' may hint at a coming change. The smell of 'honey and almonds' appeals to the senses and creates a sweet, idyllic mood.
Paragraph 4: The sky is 'hard and clear', the adjective making it seem cruel. 'The cold came down from the glacier like a thief' personifies the frost as a criminal creeping in at night to steal the harvest. Stars 'sharp as broken glass' transform the usual beauty of stars into something dangerous. The family 'coughing in the bitter smoke' shows the physical cost of their effort. Bibi Gul is 'a small bent shape in the orange glow', stressing her age and frailty, yet she touches the trunks 'as if she were comforting children', revealing how deeply she loves the trees she planted. Her breath 'like a ghost' conveys the cold and perhaps her fear of loss. 'Nobody slept' is short and emphatic.
Overall, the contrast between the idyllic blossom and the threatening night makes the partial survival in paragraph 5 deeply moving.
